I left out the claim that her findings are ready for a top journal. The facts you gave don't support it yet: the study hasn't been repeated, one site lost 3 months of data, and so far it's only been presented as a poster. Admissions committees read a lot of these letters, and a claim they can check and find too strong can make them doubt the rest of your praise. Instead, the letter makes the case that does hold up: she designed and ran a demanding 14-month field study by herself, and her results are worth following up. In marine ecology that's a strong letter.

Bracketed items are placeholders for you to fill in.

<final_document>
[Date]

Dear Members of the Admissions Committee,

I am writing to recommend Priya [Last Name] for your PhD program in marine ecology without reservation. I have taught biology at [College] for 17 years and supervised about 30 senior theses. Priya is one of the most capable and committed students I have worked with.

Priya took three courses with me: [Course 1], [Course 2], and [Course 3]. In two of them she earned the top grade in a class of 28. What set her apart was not just her command of the material but how she reasoned through it. She asked questions that showed she was already thinking about how to test ideas, not just how to learn them.

Her senior thesis, which I supervised, showed those qualities most clearly. Priya compared oyster growth at six sites in [Bay name] over 14 months. She designed the sampling scheme and did all of the fieldwork herself, about 90 trips by kayak through every season. That kind of sustained effort is unusual for an undergraduate. It takes physical endurance, careful planning, and a willingness to keep collecting data when conditions are cold, wet, and tedious. When a storm knocked out data collection at one site for three months, she documented the gap carefully and accounted for it in her analysis rather than glossing over it.

Her results were interesting: oysters grew faster at the two sites next to the salt marsh. This is a single season of data, and Priya understands that the pattern needs to be repeated and its causes investigated. In my view, the fact that she sees that clearly is itself a sign of her readiness for graduate research. She presented the work as a poster at [Conference name], where she answered questions from working scientists with confidence and precision.

Priya has also worked in a professional research setting. Last summer she was a paid field assistant at [State shellfish lab]. There she worked alongside agency scientists on [brief description of duties, if known], which gave her a realistic view of applied shellfish research and confirmed her interest in a research career.

Priya has the intellectual ability, field skills, and persistence that doctoral work in marine ecology requires. She also has a question she is eager to pursue. I am confident she will be a productive and generous member of your program, and I recommend her to you with enthusiasm.

Please feel free to contact me at [email] or [phone] if I can provide any further information.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]
[Title], Department of Biology
[College]
</final_document>

Some suggestions:
- **Add a specific moment.** One concrete example would do more than any adjective. It could be a problem she solved in the field, a sharp question she asked in class, or how she handled the storm data. Only you can supply that.
- **If a manuscript is actually in progress**, for example if you're coauthoring a paper with her, say so directly ("we are preparing a manuscript based on this work"). That's a concrete, credible statement.
- **Comparative rankings carry weight.** If it's true, something like "among the top two or three students I've supervised in 17 years" is one of the most useful lines a committee can read.
